meta.title: The Bloop: The Scientist Who Said Ice, and the World That Heard a Monster
meta.logline: In 1997 NOAA hydrophones caught a sound no one could name. The scientist running the listening said ice. The press said monster. It took eight years to settle it.
meta.thesis: The Bloop is less a sea-monster story than a story about how a careful scientific hunch gets drowned out by a better headline.
meta.curiosity_gap: Why did a sound that turned out to be ice become the world's most famous sea monster?
meta.narrator: Rzeczowy, dynamiczny narrator dokumentalny w 3. osobie. Krótkie zdania, rytm reportażu, napięcie bez sensacji. Cytaty czytane dosłownie.
meta.audience_relation: Prowadzi widza tropem bohatera (Christopher Fox) jak w reportażu śledczym; czasem 'you' na zwrotach.
meta.lexicon: hydrophones = 'the ears'; SOSUS = Sound Surveillance System
meta.bans: Zero lania wody. Żadnych zmyślonych nazwisk, dat, liczb, cytatów. Nie pokazuj obcych osób jako Foxa. Rekonstrukcje AI oznaczone.
meta.visual_style: archival documentary, desaturated, film grain, typewriter titles, black and red cards
meta.master_outline: 1) Cold open: the real sound + the conflict. 2) Cold War ears (SOSUS). 3) Fox's team turns them to science (1993 eruption). 4) Fox's library of named sounds. 5) The Bloop. 6) Fox says ice (2001) vs press says monster (2002). 7) 2005: icequake; 2008 A53a. 8) Outro.

facts.claim: In 1997 NOAA researchers listening for underwater volcanic activity in the southern Pacific recorded a mysterious sound later named 'the Bloop'.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: The Bloop was picked up by hydrophones placed more than 3,219 km apart across the Pacific.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: In the 1960s the US Navy set up an array of underwater microphones (hydrophones) around the globe, known as SOSUS (Sound Surveillance System), to track Soviet submarines.
facts.source: David Wolman, 'Calls from the deep', New Scientist, 15 June 2002

facts.claim: The end of the Cold War meant that by 1991 SOSUS could be shared with civilian scientists; in 1991 NOAA was granted access to it.
facts.source: New Scientist 2002; Fox et al., GRL 1995 (NOAA PMEL)

facts.claim: On June 22, 1993 NOAA installed a real-time monitoring system at U.S. Naval Facility Whidbey Island (Washington State); on June 26 a burst of seismic activity with harmonic tremor was detected on the Juan de Fuca Ridge, four days later; fresh lavas were subsequently found at the site.
facts.source: Fox, Radford, Dziak et al., Geophysical Research Letters 22 (1995), NOAA PMEL

facts.claim: In 2002 Christopher Fox directed NOAA's Acoustic Monitoring Project at the Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory in Newport, Oregon.
Fox named unidentified ocean sounds on a whim: Train, Whistle, Slowdown and Bloop.
Fox quote: 'Just when you think there're no mysteries left in this world, we have a whole bucket of them on the screen here.'
Fox quote to CNN, 7 September 2001: 'We're suspecting that it's ice off the coast of Antarctica, in which case it's darn loud.'
facts.source: CNN, 'Scientists tune in to sounds of the sea', 7 September 2001

facts.claim: Fox on military hydrophones used for science (CNN 2001): 'It was sort of a plowshare sort of thing.'

New Scientist (June 2002) reported: 'Fox's hunch is that the sound nicknamed Bloop is the most likely to come from some sort of animal', because its frequency varied rapidly like sounds made by marine animals.
facts.note: relacja dziennikarza; historyk P. Hayward uważa, że przeczucie zostało 'wzmocnione'

facts.claim: CNN, 13 June 2002: 'Scientists have revealed a mysterious recording that they say could be the sound of a giant beast lurking in the depths of the ocean.'
facts.source: CNN, 'Tuning in to a deep sea monster', 13 June 2002

facts.claim: Fox quote (New Scientist 2002): 'There's a blue whale, there's a fin whale, there's a boat, there's a humpback whale and here comes an earthquake.' He could identify most sounds by their spectrogram alone.
Popular claims said the Bloop was much louder than a blue whale, the loudest known animal.
facts.source: Popular Science — The sea monster goes 'bloop'—or does it?

facts.claim: In 2005, after placing hydrophones closer to Antarctica, NOAA researchers found the Bloop was an icequake: an iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: NOAA's public recording of the Bloop is sped up 16 times so human ears can hear it.
Icequakes are loud enough to be detected on multiple sensors at a range of over 5,000 km.
NOAA hydrophones in the Scotia Sea recorded icequakes very similar to the Bloop and used them to track iceberg A53a as it broke apart near South Georgia Island in early 2008.
Fox (CNN 2001) on what hydrophones hear: 'Whales, dolphins and fish, the rumblings of the Earth.'
Reconstruction: fresh lava on the seafloor (AI image).
Based on the direction the sound arrived from, NOAA estimates the Bloop source was most likely between the Bransfield Strait and the Ross Sea, or possibly at Cape Adare, Antarctica.

SOFAR is a natural ocean channel that lets low-frequency sound bounce between layers and travel hundreds, sometimes thousands of miles; hydrophones placed at the channel axis (typically around 1 km deep, varying with latitude) record distant sounds.
facts.source: NOAA Ocean Service — What is SOFAR?; NOAA PMEL

beats.action: Breath: two stories, nine months apart; only way to know is to get closer. Then 2005 icequake; 2008 A53a — play real NOAA audio.
beats.goal: Viewer gets the answer and hears ice breaking.
beats.narration: Two stories. One scientist. Nine months apart. Ice, or something alive. The only way to know was to get closer. So NOAA did. Researchers placed hydrophones nearer to Antarctica, and in 2005 they had the answer. The Bloop was an icequake: an iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier. Three years later, the same kind of listening followed an iceberg called A53a as it broke apart near South Georgia Island. This is what that sounded like.

beats.link: In 2005 NOAA confirmed the Bloop was an icequake, and in 2008 the same listening tracked iceberg A53a breaking apart.
beats.raw:
Narracja:
Two stories. One scientist. Nine months apart. Ice, or something alive. The only way to know was to get closer. So NOAA did. Researchers placed hydrophones nearer to Antarctica, and in 2005 they had the answer. The Bloop was an icequake: an iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier. Three years later, the same kind of listening followed an iceberg called A53a as it broke apart near South Georgia Island. This is what that sounded like.
